claim: Cloudera's CFM, CSA and CSM Operator requirement/release-notes pages make no statement about CPU architecture at all; arm64 support for CSO is neither confirmed nor denied by Cloudera, and only the upstream components (Strimzi >=0.27.0, apache/nifi 2.x images, Apache Flink K8s Operator) are documented multi-arch.

votes.note: The claim is refuted: Cloudera's own CFM Operator installation docs explicitly provide a linux/arm64 binary download, listing "https://archive.cloudera.com/p/cfm-operator/cfmctl-linux-arm64" alongside cfmctl-darwin-arm64 and cfmctl-windows-arm64 — this is a direct, primary-source statement about CPU architecture support for the cfmctl CLI, contradicting "make no statement about CPU architecture at all." Note this is the cfmctl client binary, not necessarily the operator's controller/pod container image, so it doesn't fully settle whether the in-cluster operator workload itself is multi-arch — but it does falsify the blanket "no statement about CPU architecture" claim. (The CSA Operator release-notes page and the csm-operator system-req page, by contrast, were confirmed to say nothing about architecture.)

No first-hand community evidence (forum thread, GitHub issue, reddit, X post with a real run) was found either confirming or denying arm64/DGX-Spark support for the CFM/CSA/CSM Kubernetes Operator container images. The only arm64-related hit is Cloudera's own docs noting arm64 builds of the `cfmctl` CLI tool (darwin/linux/windows-arm64) — a client binary, not the operator/NiFi container images, and it's vendor documentation, not community-empirical evidence anyway. NVIDIA's own DGX Spark developer forum shows unrelated third-party containers (RAG blueprint, nv-ingest) hitting arm64 "exec format error" failures, which is suggestive of general ecosystem immaturity but says nothing about Cloudera's operators specifically. Under the community-empirical lens, no evidence was found to refute or confirm the claim, so per instructions I default to refuted=true with low confidence.

Cloudera's own CFM Operator installation docs list a cfmctl-linux-arm64 download alongside linux-amd64, darwin-arm64, darwin-amd64, and windows-amd64 — i.e. Cloudera documents arm64 support directly for its own operator tooling, not just upstream components. This contradicts the claim's assertion that Cloudera's requirement/release-notes pages "make no statement about CPU architecture at all" and that arm64 is "neither confirmed nor denied." Note: the specific CSM system-requirements page cited as the source does indeed omit architecture text (confirmed), but the broader claim about the whole operator family is refuted by the CFM install page, which is a Cloudera-authored requirement/installation doc, current as of 2.8.0/2.10.0 lines still live in docs.cloudera.com in 2026.

claim: On GB10 the classic NVIDIA k8s device plugin crashes because nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo returns 'Not Supported' under unified memory; the fix is k8s-device-plugin v0.17.4 or newer (whose release note reads 'Ignore errors getting device memory using NVML'), and MIG is unavailable so time-slicing is the only GPU-sharing mechanism.

votes.note: Primary-source confirmation for the device-plugin fix: NVIDIA's own k8s-device-plugin v0.17.4 GitHub release notes state "Ignore errors getting device memory using NVML" (PR #1374 by @elezar), matching the claim's mechanism and fix version exactly. The MIG-unavailable-on-GB10 leg is not explicitly stated in NVIDIA's official MIG User Guide (docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide) — GB10/DGX Spark/Grace Blackwell superchip simply do not appear in that guide's supported-GPU table at all (only A100/A30/H100/H200/B200/RTX PRO 6000/5000 Blackwell are listed), which is consistent with but does not prove non-support. Driver 580.95.05/CUDA 12.x vs NVIDIA's stated 580.159.03/CUDA 13.0.2 discrepancy was not independently re-verified in this pass. Overall: not refuted — the core, checkable technical claim (NVML memory-info fix in v0.17.4) is verified against NVIDIA's own primary release notes; the MIG-unavailability claim is plausible but only indirectly supported by primary docs (absence from the support table), not an explicit vendor statement.

First-hand GitHub issue (NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin#1482) independently confirms the core mechanism: device plugin fails on GB10 with "error getting device memory: Not Supported", and nvidia-smi also reports "Not Supported" for memory on GB10 — matching the claim's NVML/unified-memory failure mode without relying on the collabnix blog. A parallel first-hand issue (kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu#1073, titled "GPU plugin fails on DGX Spark (GB10) — nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo returns 'Not Supported'") and Project-HAMi/HAMi#1511 corroborate the same symptom across multiple independent community repos. I could not directly verify the v0.17.4 fix text or the MIG-unavailable/time-slicing-only claim from a first-hand source within budget (search summaries mention v0.17.4 and time-slicing but I did not fetch a primary changelog or forum thread confirming those specifics verbatim), so confidence is medium rather than high — the core NVML/GB10 failure claim is refuted-false (i.e., supported), but the version-fix and MIG-unavailability sub-claims remain only search-summarized, not directly quoted from a primary source.

No staleness found: k8s-device-plugin releases continued past v0.17.4 (through v0.19.x/v0.20.0) and the NVML-memory-error tolerance fix persisted forward rather than being reverted or superseded by a different mechanism. MIG-on-GB10 unavailability is also still current — NVIDIA developer forum threads through late 2025 confirm "DGX Spark does not support MIG, vGPU, NVSwitch, or Fabric Manager... single GPU on a desktop SoC." One inconsistency worth flagging to the user: a GitHub releases fetch attributed the "Ignore errors getting device memory using NVML" changelog line to v0.18.1 rather than v0.17.4 as the collabnix post claims — the exact version number should be confirmed directly against https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/releases since automated summarization here produced internally inconsistent dates.

claim: k3d with GPU is not documented on any DGX Spark; k3d's own CUDA guide says the stock k3s node image is Alpine-based, 'the NVIDIA container runtime is not supported on Alpine yet', so a custom CUDA-base node image with runtimeClassName: nvidia is required — whereas plain k3s (--docker or containerd) is proven on real GB10 hardware by multiple sources.

votes.note: k3d's own docs (a primary project source) state verbatim: "The native K3s image is based on Alpine but the NVIDIA container runtime is not supported on Alpine yet," requiring a custom CUDA-base image and "you must explicitly add runtimeClassName: nvidia to all your Pod specs to use the GPU" — confirming the claim exactly. Searches of NVIDIA's own DGX Spark docs (docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/) found only Docker/NVIDIA Container Runtime and K3s coverage, with no NVIDIA primary-source page documenting k3d (vs plain k3s) GPU support on GB10 hardware — nothing under the primary-docs lens refutes the claim.

Community-empirical search finds no first-hand thread of k3d's Docker-in-Docker GPU path actually run on real DGX Spark/GB10 hardware. The NVIDIA Developer Forums thread "Local Kubernetes Cluster with K3s on Nvidia DGX Spark" is plain k3s with Docker configured to use the NVIDIA Container Runtime directly on the host — not k3d — matching the claim's assertion that proven recipes are k3s, not k3d. This supports rather than refutes the claim under the community-empirical lens; I could not find contrary first-hand evidence within the search budget.

The k3d docs (checked live, latest version) still state verbatim: "The native K3s image is based on Alpine but the NVIDIA container runtime is not supported on Alpine yet," requiring a custom CUDA-base image with runtimeClassName: nvidia. A broader web search for 2026 updates found no change — the actively maintained 88plug/k3d-gpu project (early 2026) confirms this is still the workaround pattern, not a superseded limitation. No newer k3d release note or GPU-native fix was found.

claim: Cloudera AI Inference on-premises entered Technical Preview on 2025-08-07 with Cloudera Data Services 1.5.5, and the 2026-02-09 press release says it is 'now available on-premises, accelerated by NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, Dynamo-Triton and NIM' — without using the words GA or Technical Preview.

votes.note: Partially refuted on a factual detail: Cloudera's own press release for the on-prem AI Inference "Technical Preview" milestone is dated 2025-08-06, not 2025-08-07 as the claim states (https://www.cloudera.com/about/news-and-blogs/press-releases/2025-08-06-cloudera-data-services-brings-private-ai-to-the-data-center.html), and that release does not actually use the words "Technical Preview" anywhere in its text — it just says AI Inference on-prem "is one of the industry's first AI inference services," with no explicit maturity label. However, the claim's core assertion about the 2026-02-09 release is confirmed accurate: that page states Cloudera AI Inference is "now available on premises," "Accelerated by ... NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton Inference Server, and NVIDIA NIM microservices," with neither "GA" nor "Technical Preview" appearing in the fetched text.

No first-hand community evidence (forum threads with real runs, GitHub issues, reddit, X posts) could be found confirming or refuting on-prem CAII's actual production status or real deployments with Blackwell/Dynamo-Triton/NIM. Search results returned only vendor press coverage (Cloudera itself, ITBrief, ITBeat, CloudNews) and Cloudera's own community forum announcement post — no independent practitioner accounts of running on-prem CAII. Under the community-empirical lens (vendor marketing excluded), there is no supporting evidence within the fetch budget, so the claim is treated as refuted by default per instructions.

Could not find a newer Cloudera source (docs.cloudera.com/machine-learning/1.5.5 on-prem docs, or CDP-cloud release notes) that explicitly labels on-prem Cloudera AI Inference as "GA" or "Technical Preview" as of Aug 2026, so the claim's core observation — that Cloudera's own language stays ambiguous — still holds. Note: docs.cloudera.com/machine-learning/cloud/release-notes lists a "June 18, 2026 (GA)" entry, but that page tree is Cloudera AI on CDP public cloud, not the on-prem/private-cloud Data Services 1.5.5+ product the claim concerns, so it doesn't resolve the on-prem ambiguity either way. I did not directly fetch the CAII auth/API docs page, so this remains unresolved rather than confirmed.

claim: Realistic single-DGX-Spark interactive decode for 20B-120B MoE models is roughly 45-61 tok/s (llama.cpp: GPT-OSS-120B ~60.6 tok/s, GPT-OSS-20B ~60.9, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q8 ~44.3), dropping to ~40 tok/s at 32K context; dense FP16 models are far slower (Qwen3-32B ~3.5 tok/s on early vLLM) and only speculative decoding pushes small MoE much higher (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 176.66 tok/s reproduced vs 202.63 claimed).

votes.note: NVIDIA's own developer blog confirms the 273 GB/s bandwidth invariant and puts GPT-OSS-120B at 55.37 tok/s (llama.cpp, MXFP4) — close to the claimed ~60.6. But it lists GPT-OSS-20B at 82.74 tok/s, well above the claim's ~60.9, and gives no primary-source figures for Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B or dense Qwen3-32B, so the claim is only partially corroborated by vendor docs, not refuted outright.

The cited llama.cpp discussion #16578 corroborates the MoE decode-speed core of the claim: GPT-OSS-120B tg32 ~60.57 tok/s, GPT-OSS-20B tg32 ~65 tok/s (close to claimed 60.9), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q8 tg32 ~48 tok/s (close to claimed 44.3), and GPT-OSS-120B drops to tg ~40.55 tok/s at d32768 context — matching the claimed "~40 tok/s at 32K context" almost exactly. This is first-hand community benchmark data (a GitHub discussion of real llama.cpp runs on DGX Spark), satisfying the community-empirical lens. However, the discussion contains no data on dense Qwen3-32B FP16 (~3.5 tok/s) or the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 speculative-decoding figures (176.66 vs 202.63) cited in the claim — those specific sub-claims are not verifiable from this source and were not found via search, so confidence is medium rather than high.

2026 search results corroborate rather than refute: the llama.cpp discussion's gpt-oss-120b MXFP4 figures (60.6 tok/s gen, dropping to 40.6 at 32K context) are echoed by a Dec 2025 benchmark (59.05 tok/s at batch 32) and multiple 2026 secondary sources citing the same 273 GB/s bandwidth ceiling as invariant. No newer llama.cpp/vLLM/SGLang release was found that supersedes these numbers; SGLang is reported ~13% faster (52 tok/s) but that's a different-engine comparison, not a staleness refutation of the original claim.

claim: NVIDIA (APAC, 2026-07-14) states a 4-node DGX Spark cluster supports inference on models up to 700B parameters with 'near-linear' scaling for fine-tuning/RL — while independent 4-node GLM-5.2 (744B) deployments measure 23-48 tok/s decode at 250K-655K context, and vLLM tensor-parallel-size 2 across two Sparks is reported unstable.

votes.note: NVIDIA's own developer blog on DGX Spark multi-node clustering states four nodes provide 512 GB unified memory, framed as supporting large MoE models/fine-tuning jobs — it does not state a "700B parameter" ceiling or quantify "near-linear scaling for fine-tuning/RL" as the claim asserts. The 400B/512GB framing is consistent with a 2-node=~400B extrapolation, but the specific 700B and near-linear-scaling language appears nowhere in NVIDIA's primary documentation I could find; it traces to the cited tweet, not a doc, confirming the claim's own caveat.

Community-empirical evidence corroborates the claim's counterweight framing. tonyd2wild's own repo BENCHMARKS.md (GLM-5.2-NVFP4-KV-4x-DGX-Spark-300kctx-42tok-s) and 0xdfi's "GLM-5.2-1M-4x-DGX-Spark" repo report measured decode throughput in the 21.5-42 tok/s range across 2-4 node DGX Spark clusters at large context (200K-1M), not the smooth "near-linear scaling" NVIDIA's tweet implies — e.g. 2x Spark nodes only hit ~15-21.5 tok/s with 2-bit quantization, and even the best 4-node NVFP4 recipe tops out at 42 tok/s peak (32.5 mean). These are hand-built, quantization-dependent recipes (custom Triton/CuTe kernels "built in one night," per Tech2Wild's X post) rather than out-of-the-box vendor performance, which is direct first-hand evidence the 700B-scale "near-linear" vendor claim omits the real measured ceiling and instability community builders hit.

The NVIDIAAP tweet (2026-07-14) is real and matches verbatim: "scales up to four clustered nodes, enabling inference on models up to 700B parameters — with near-linear performance scaling for fine-tuning and reinforcement learning workloads." No newer NVIDIA statement supersedes this. Community counterweights confirmed current: 0xdfi/Tech2Wild report 42 tok/s peak decode (744B GLM-5.2, 4x Spark, NVFP4), NVIDIA dev forum reports ~22 tok/s at 256K context, and light_foundry's 48 tok/s figure is on an 8x cluster, not 4x — so the guide's counterweight framing holds and nothing is stale.
